title: Supervised Learning for Urban Prediction
topicSummary: Classification, regression, decision trees, support vector machines (SVM) etc. Case studies.

content.text: This module focuses on Supervised Learning, the most widely used machine learning paradigm in urban analytics.
Objective: Predict outcomes using labeled data, understand key algorithms, and apply them to real-world prediction problems.
Definition: Supervised learning uses a dataset where inputs (features) and outputs (labels/targets) are already known.
👉 The model learns a mapping: X → y
Example: Input (Time, location, vehicle count) → Output (Traffic congestion level).
Definition: Used when the output is continuous (numerical).
Example: Predict traffic speed, Predict pollution level.
Definition: Used when the output is categorical (classes).
Example: Traffic condition (Low / Medium / High), Accident risk (Yes / No).

📖 Reading Note: A useful way to choose between regression and classification: Ask yourself — 'Is the answer a number or a category?' Predicting tomorrow's PM2.5 level (like 87.3 μg/m³) → Regression. Predicting whether tomorrow's air quality is 'Good', 'Moderate', or 'Hazardous' → Classification. Interestingly, you can sometimes convert a regression problem into a classification problem by thresholding: if predicted PM2.5 > 60 → classify as 'Unhealthy'. This is done in practice when city systems need to trigger binary alerts.
Definition: A tree-based model that splits data based on conditions.
Example: If traffic > 50 → High congestion; Else → Low congestion.

items: Advantages: Easy to understand, works with both classification and regression.
Limitations: Can overfit, sensitive to data changes.

content.text: 📖 Reading Note: Decision Trees are both a practical ML model and a policy communication tool. A city traffic department can show a Decision Tree to non-technical stakeholders: 'If hour < 9am AND day = weekday → increase green signal at arterial junctions by 30s.' This is machine-learned logic written in plain English. Random Forest (an ensemble of many Decision Trees) dramatically reduces overfitting by averaging predictions from 100+ trees, each trained on a random data subset. It's one of the most reliable algorithms for urban tabular data.
Definition: SVM finds the optimal boundary (hyperplane) that separates data into classes by maximizing the margin between them.

items: Features: Works well in high-dimensional data, effective for classification.

content.text: 📖 Reading Note: SVM's 'kernel trick' is key to its power. By using a kernel function (like RBF — Radial Basis Function), SVM can classify data that is not linearly separable — it projects data into a higher-dimensional space where a hyperplane can be found. In urban terms: classifying which road segments will become 'high congestion zones' based on a mix of road geometry, nearby population density, and temporal patterns is not a linearly separable problem. The RBF kernel lets SVM handle this complexity. Kernel='rbf' is a single parameter in scikit-learn's SVC class.

items: Case Study 1 (Traffic Congestion): Input: Vehicle count, time, road type → Model: Regression → Output: Congestion level.
Case Study 2 (Accident Risk): Input: Weather, speed, road condition → Model: Decision Tree / SVM → Output: Risk category.
Case Study 3 (Air Quality): Input: Emissions, weather data → Model: Regression → Output: AQI value.

content.text: 📖 Reading Note: A published real-world case — Los Angeles DOT built a supervised learning model (Random Forest regressor) using 3 years of intersection-level data (vehicle counts, signal timing, time of day, weather) to predict Travel Time Index (TTI) — a congestion measure. The model achieved RMSE of 0.08 (very accurate) and is now used in their ATSAC (Automated Traffic Surveillance and Control) system to pre-adjust signal timings 15 minutes before predicted peak congestion. This proactive approach reduced average peak travel times by 11%.

content.text: How Week 7 Concepts Connect Across the Course:

rows: Linear regression uses the MSE loss function introduced in Week 6 — Week 7 puts the theory into a specific algorithm
LSTM time-series models predict continuous values (e.g., next hour's traffic count) — a temporal extension of the regression concept from Week 7
CNNs perform image classification (vehicle type = car/bus/truck) — the classification framework from Week 7 scales to image data in Week 9
Random Forest (an ensemble of Decision Trees) is unsupervised extension of Week 7's trees — hierarchical clustering in Week 8 shares similar tree structures
SVM's hyperplane equation (w·x + b = 0) directly uses the linear algebra concepts from Week 6's foundational theories section
The traffic congestion and AQI prediction models from Week 7's case studies are embedded in the integrated smart city dashboards of Week 12

content.text: 🔗 Big Picture: Week 7 is the 'predictive toolkit' of the course. Regression and Classification are the two most-used ML paradigms in urban informatics — nearly every smart city data problem can be framed as one or the other. Everything learned here (algorithms, workflow, evaluation) applies directly to Week 8 (pattern discovery) and Week 9 (deep learning).
